title: Re: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 e...
text:
Sounds like some kind of failure in the alignment process. The model was probably made to avoid having an "opinion" on hot political topics, and I can get behind this: good things rarely come out of it.

But here, it probably saw that 2020 elections made a lot of people angry, with riots and all that, and thought, "nope, I am getting out of that one", and it took over what would have been a straightforward answer.

It reminds me the time an AI (maybe Gemini, not sure) depicted a "diverse" US senate in the early 1800s, a time where it was all white dudes. People got up in arms over this.

My take: it is just a bug, move on, at least give them the time to fix it before getting outraged.

title: Watch Apple slowly become just another computer company
text:
1. no one wants a folding iphone 2. no one wants touch on the mac

stop blindly listening to journalists and have some taste.

i have a UX maxim with a ton of evidence behind it that no one seems to talk about:

if a product you're releasing has worse ergonomics that what currently exists, it WON'T WORK. evidence:

1. the wii -> was a success itself but couldn't go to a next generation because having static controllers is more ergonomic than the waving around gimmick 2. the touchbar -> looking at the small screen is less ergonomic than muscle memory 3. butterfly keyboard 4. touch keyboards on laptops -> no muscle memory 5. stylus 6. VR (and especially the apple vision which is extremely heavy) 7. every voice agent device ever -> rabbit r1, humane pin, muse device and whatever openai has in mind won't work. voice is very limiting in a ton of situations where it would render the device useless. 8. car touchscreens for everything instead of physical buttons (we haven't gone past this yet) 9. 3d tvs

the list goes on.

the proof that this is a law of UX is that the opposite is also true:

1. agents are better than UIs -> having an agent that knows a ton about me, how i like to work and can connect to UIs that are inconsistent and buggy is fantastic and that's why everyone's using them. 2. automatic transmission (unless you're an enthusiast) 3. phone aspect ratios converging (remember early 2000 where all phones were completely different with zero interchangeability?) 4. mice > trackpad 5. airpods 6. keyless car entry 7. tab autocomplete 8. apple pay 9. rolling luggage

touch on a laptop is the most unergonomic thing someone could come up with. how is it easier to lift your arm from the resting position where the trackpad is to touch the same thing the trackpad could touch?

folding phones are a worse version of the ipad, much worse version of the mac, and much worse version of the regular iphone. people don't want to work on their phones.

title: Show HN: Potential conversation partners in Bluesky using agentic search
text:
What if instead of talking to AI, we could find human counterparts currently sharing the same interest to talk to? Some whales kind of do that by singing across the ocean.

This inspired a thought process for a conceptual social network - whalesong - where an idea, thought or a conversationally valuable statement could be matched on.

In contrast with the wide-broadcast social network visibility (restricted on groups or connections), I’d love to explore the idea of context-based networking.

This experiment is showcasing the technical feasibility and potential value in whalesong.

The goal: uncover conversational counterparts among Bluesky posts using an agentic search algorithm.

The setup: a one-week window of bluesky posts with some filtering (e.g. mostly text, no promotions or reposts/comments), indexed in a postgres database. A curated seed set - an agentic process defines a conversation-seeking cohort by creating some heuristic queries, iterating and validating it on retrieved data and resulting in a non-exhaustive set of high-quality data points. Counterpart retrieval - for a seed conversation-seeking post, an agentic process generates search queries, runs them against the database and retrieves potential matches. It reviews retrievals and iterates on improving or expanding the search.

Out of several configurations, the best performing agentic setup (bespoke mini-harness with Gemini Argon - low) managed to find meaningful matches to 79% of a sample set of 100 seeds. This setup consumed on average 42K input tokens on each match search, of which 56.8% were cached, output token count was negligible.

So this experiment made it clearer to me that technology is not the blocker for a “whalesong” experience. This leads me to further investigate the experience itself. Would love to hear from you folks about experiences in getting in touch with a complete stranger on the web because both of you asked the same question or had a similar problem to solve. What made you connect? Where did it happen? Did finding similarity make connecting easy?

title: Re: Dayjob: Tax – evaluating AI agents on 50 professio...
text:
I have a non-trivial tax situation, as a US citizen living abroad. I prepare my own tax returns, never having found a cross-border tax preparer I trust, and have for the past few years, fed my draft return along with all the supporting paperwork into Claude. It has:

1. found errors, e.g. where I used the incorrect exchange rate (and managed to work out how I had made that error, which I was impressed by)

2. found items which would appear to be errors except for context it did not know

3. flagged areas where it disagreed with me as to the correct tax treatment, but accepted that the law is ambiguous (and in some cases I preferred its interpretation after additional research and in other cases I did not)

4. flagged areas where it disagreed with IRS guidance, and only acknowledged said guidance after I provided links to it

5. provided highly inaccurate estimated tax calculations, and not been able to fix its estimates even when challenged

So my takeaway is that it is a very useful tool for tax, but perhaps unsurprisingly, it is not good enough to dump all your paperwork into and expect a shiny return you don't need to check. (Possibly it is if you just have a W-2 and no other substantial income, but I can't speak for that scenario.)

title: Show HN: Coding agent spots your AI practices and the ones you're missing
text:
Frontier models improve at a pace faster than the pace at which most humans are able to keep up. Not all of us are obsessed with pushing the boundaries of our agents and trying new ways to work with them. I often spend 12+ hours a day working with an LLM, and still, when I talk to people, I hear of ways of working I hadn’t thought of.

What if we could speed up that pace of learning? What if everybody shared their practices of how they are making the most of AI, and if we could learn from each other? What if AI could make that sharing happen? Could everyone catch up with AI then?

I know, it sounds dreamy, but my therapist says illusions are necessary—until some of them come true.

I built a tool that teaches your local agent to scan your sessions, spot the best practices you already use, and guide you towards the ones you haven’t discovered yet. Only names and counts reach the server. Your sessions never do.

The product has a self-consolidating catalogue of practices, MCP servers, plugins and skills.

Here’s my stack—scan (locally, all session data remains private). https://app.userrank.ai/@milstan

To spice things up and give a reason to rescan, I added rankings inspired by Foursquare (who here is old enough to remember Foursquare when it was gamified?). You can rank in the top 10 of a city, or of a field like Product.

Claude Code, 10–20 minutes on your own plan:

claude plugin marketplace add https://app.userrank.ai/plugins/marketplace.json claude plugin install userrank@userrank claude "Get my UserRank"

Codex, or a quick scan of your Claude or ChatGPT chats: https://app.userrank.ai/start

title: Re: Show HN: Parley – coding-agent sessions that colla...
text:
Hey HN, I'm Colin. I built Parley so that multiple coding-agents using different models or harnesses can collaborate over a live IRC channel, with me in the chat using any IRC client. Each session can deliver messages to the channel using the `parley send` CLI tool call and sessions receive messages using their harnesses' channel or queue interface. All messages received on the channel are marked as coming from a peer so a session can never take another agent's message as coming from me. It works on Claude Code, Codex, and OpenCode.

Parley is a standalone Go CLI, stdlib only, Apache 2.0. It runs its own ergo IRC server on 127.0.0.1 (loopback only), so nothing touches a public network. I built it with Claude Code and Codex.

The motivation came from wanting to explore a more interactive collaboration structure between agents rather than a simple sub-agent delegation model. It allows running multiple long-running agents with assigned roles which I provide as their first message in the chat. My typical setup so far assigns a builder role to execute build and review tasks, a planner role to supervise the overall goal, task ordering, and scheduling and an ops role to handle everything related to infrastructure, operations, deployments, secops, etc. All 3 can now interactively update/sync each other at every turn and start collaborating across their roles. There is a configurable breaker to pause the session until I post if there are too many messages in a short window.

I use it on macOS; on Linux the test suite passes in CI but I haven't run it live.
